mainEntity.name: Why aren’t percentage increases and decreases symmetrical?

acceptedAnswer.text: Percentage change is measured against the starting value. Going from 100 to 125 is +25%; going from 125 back to 100 is −25 ÷ 125 = −20%, because the base is now 125. A 25% increase therefore needs a 20% decrease to return to the original.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between percentage points and percent change?

acceptedAnswer.text: Percentage points are the simple difference between two percentages: going from 4% to 5% is 1 percentage point. Percent change compares them proportionally: 5 is 25% more than 4. Mixing the two up is a common source of misleading headlines.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate a discount before sales tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the price by (1 − discount rate) to get the sale price, then multiply by (1 + tax rate). For $80 with 25% off and 8% tax: 80 × 0.75 × 1.08 = $64.80. Some jurisdictions tax the pre-discount price in certain cases, so check the local rules.

mainEntity.name: How do I find the original price before a percentage change?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the final value by the growth factor. After a 20% discount the factor is 0.80, so a $120 price came from 120 ÷ 0.80 = $150. Subtracting 20% of $120 would give the wrong answer.

mainEntity.name: Can a percentage be greater than 100%?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. 150% of a number is one and a half times it, and a value that doubles has increased by 100%. Only percentages of a fixed whole (such as a share of a total) are limited to 100%.

mainEntity.name: What if the starting value is zero?

acceptedAnswer.text: Percentage change from zero is undefined because it divides by zero, and “X is what percent of 0” is undefined for the same reason. Report the absolute change instead.
